extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent applicants/patent practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and resolving indefiniteness and means-plus-function issues in patent claims under 35 U.S.C. § 112 (¶¶ 2, 4, and 6), including functional language, terms of degree, subjective terms, Markush groups, dependent claims, and computer-implemented limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine Whether Each Claim Limitation Invokes 35 U.S.C. 112, ¶6
rubrics_metrics.description: As part of the claim interpretation analysis, examiners should determine whether each limitation invokes 35 U.S.C. 112, ¶ 6 (means-plus-function) or not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim limitation invokes 112, ¶ 6, the claim limitation must "be construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof." See PART 1, section III.C for more information regarding the determination and means-plus-function claim limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definiteness under § 112, ¶ 2
rubrics_metrics.description: A decision on whether a claim is indefinite requires determining whether those skilled in the art would understand what is claimed when the claim is read in light of the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim terms are typically given their ordinary and customary meaning as understood by one of ordinary skill in the pertinent art; analyze claim terms in view of the specification from the perspective of those skilled in the relevant art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional Claiming (when claim recites what it does rather than what it is)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim term is functional when it recites a feature 'by what it does rather than by what it is.' §112, ¶6 expressly authorizes a form of functional claiming (means-plus-function), and functional language can be used outside means-plus-function format (structure followed by function).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functional language is permissible but may be indefinite if it fails to provide a clear-cut indication of scope (e.g., merely stating a problem to be solved or a result achieved) or if it encompasses all means/methods without reciting structure/material/steps. Such unlimited functional limitations may lack written description or enablement under §112, ¶1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors for Determining Ambiguity of Functional Language
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim limitation employs functional language, the examiner’s determination of whether the limitation is sufficiently definite depends on context (specification disclosure and knowledge of a person of ordinary skill).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider (1) whether there is a clear-cut indication of the scope covered by the claim; (2) whether the language sets forth well-defined boundaries or only states a problem/result; and (3) whether one of ordinary skill in the art would know from the claim terms what structure or steps are encompassed. These are examples and not exhaustive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies for Ambiguous Functional Limitations During Prosecution
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant may resolve ambiguities of a functional limitation in multiple ways during prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include: (1) using a quantitative metric (numeric limitation); (2) providing a formula and examples that meet and do not meet the limitation; (3) providing general guidelines and examples sufficient for a skilled person to determine when the limitation is satisfied; or (4) amending the claims to recite the particular structure that accomplishes the function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terms of Degree
rubrics_metrics.description: When a term of degree is used in the claim, the examiner should determine whether the specification provides some standard for measuring that degree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification lacks a standard, determine whether one of ordinary skill could nevertheless ascertain the scope (e.g., recognized art standard, figures). The claim is not indefinite if the specification provides examples or teachings usable to measure the degree. An applicant may submit a 37 CFR 1.132 declaration showing examples and non-examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjective Terms
rubrics_metrics.description: When a subjective term is used in the claim, the examiner should determine whether the specification supplies some objective standard for measuring the term's scope, similar to analysis for a term of degree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some objective standard must be provided to allow the public to determine scope; dependence solely on unrestrained subjective opinion may render the claim indefinite. Applicant may overcome rejection by evidence that a skilled person can ascertain meaning from the disclosure or by amending to remove the subjective term (example: Datamize 'aesthetically pleasing' held indefinite).

rubrics_metrics.name: Markush Groups
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'Markush' claim recites a list of alternatively useable species (e.g., 'selected from the group consisting of A, B, and C'); such claims are not necessarily indefinite for breadth, but may be in certain circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A Markush group may be indefinite if so expansive that skilled persons cannot determine the metes and bounds due to inability to envision all members. Under compact prosecution, examiner should require election of species for search/examination and extend search to species that share a single structural similarity and common use when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improper Markush Grouping Doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: A Markush claim contains an 'improper Markush grouping' if the species do not share a 'single structural similarity' or a common use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Single structural similarity means membership in the same recognized physical/chemical or art-recognized class; common use means disclosed in the specification or known to be functionally equivalent. Examiner should reject for improper grouping until applicant amends to include only species sharing the similarity/use or shows they do share it. Claim may be rejected under §112, ¶2 and/or improper grouping doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent Claims Must Comply with § 112, ¶ 4
rubrics_metrics.description: Dependent claims must contain a reference to a previous claim in the same application, specify a further limitation of the subject matter claimed, and necessarily include all the limitations of the previous claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a dependent claim omits an element from its base claim or fails to add a limitation, the examiner should reject the dependent claim under §112, ¶4 (unpatentable), rather than merely objecting as a form matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correspondence Between Specification and Claims / Antecedent Basis (37 CFR 1.75(d)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification should serve as a glossary to claim terms so examiners and the public can ascertain their meaning; claim terms must find clear support or antecedent basis in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exact claim terms are not required if specification provides needed guidance via equivalent terms. Express definitions (glossaries) are encouraged as best practice. If needed support or antecedent basis is missing, object under 37 CFR 1.75(d)(1) and require amendment to description or claim amendments (without introducing new matter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal Consistency Between Claim and Specification
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim, although clear on its face, may be indefinite when a conflict or inconsistency between the claimed subject matter and the specification disclosure renders scope uncertain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include claim terms contradicted by specification definitions or examples; examiner should treat internally inconsistent claims as indefinite and explain why in Office action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption that 'means for' or 'step for' Invokes § 112, ¶ 6
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim limitation is presumed to invoke §112, ¶6 when it explicitly uses the phrase 'means for' or 'step for' and includes functional language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: That presumption is overcome when the limitation further includes the structure necessary to perform the recited function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption that Absence of 'means for' or 'step for' Does Not Invoke § 112, ¶ 6
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim limitation that does not use 'means for' or 'step for' triggers the rebuttable presumption that §112, ¶6 does not apply; this presumption is strong and not readily overcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It may be overcome if the claim uses a non-structural term that is a nonce word or verbal construct substituting for 'means for' and is associated with functional language, unless the term is understood by a skilled person to name structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-structural Terms That May Invoke §112, ¶6 and Structural Terms That Do Not
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should determine whether a claim uses non-structural terms (which may invoke ¶6) or structural terms (which do not).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-structural examples that may invoke ¶6 include 'mechanism for,' 'module for,' 'device for,' 'unit for,' 'component for,' 'element for,' 'member for,' 'apparatus for,' 'machine for,' or 'system for' (list not exhaustive). Structural terms found not to invoke ¶6 include 'circuit for,' 'detent mechanism,' 'digital detector for,' 'reciprocating member,' 'connector assembly,' 'perforation,' 'sealingly connected joints,' and 'eyeglass hanger member.' A structural modifier preceding a non-structural term (e.g., 'detent mechanism') can avoid invocation of ¶6; a non-structural modifier does not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tests to Determine Whether a Word/Term/Phrase Denotes Structure
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine whether a term coupled with a function denotes structure, examiners should check whether the specification and external evidence indicate structural meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check (1) whether the specification provides a description sufficient to inform one of ordinary skill that the term denotes structure; (2) whether general or subject-matter dictionaries provide evidence the term is recognized as a noun denoting structure; and (3) whether the prior art provides evidence the term has an art-recognized structure to perform the claimed function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions Under Which Examiners Will Apply §112, ¶6
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners will apply §112, ¶6 to a claim limitation that meets certain conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply ¶6 when (1) the claim uses 'means for'/'step for' or a non-structural term without a structural modifier; (2) the phrase or non-structural term is modified by functional language; and (3) the phrase or non-structural term is not modified by sufficient structure, material, or acts to achieve the specified function. Note: this guideline modifies the 3-prong analysis in MPEP §2181.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejections Under §112, ¶2 When Examining Means-Plus-Function Limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a claim limitation is determined to be a means-plus-function limitation invoking §112, ¶6, the examiner should determine the claimed function and then review the written description to identify corresponding structure/material/acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The disclosure must be reviewed from the viewpoint of one skilled in the art to determine whether the written description discloses the corresponding structure/material/acts and clearly links them to the claimed function. Rejection under §112, ¶2 is appropriate if there is no disclosure or insufficient disclosure, or no clear link/association. A bare statement that known techniques can be used is insufficient. Examiner may require information under 37 CFR 1.105 to identify corresponding structure; failure to identify supports rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of Means-Plus-Function Limitations When Supported
rubrics_metrics.description: If the written description sets forth the corresponding structure/material/acts in compliance with §112, ¶2, the claim limitation must be construed to cover the corresponding structure/material/acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functional limitations not recited in the claim, or structural limitations in the specification that are unnecessary to perform the claimed function, cannot be imported into the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer-Implemented Means-Plus-Function Limitations Require an Algorithm
rubrics_metrics.description: For a computer-implemented means-plus-function claim invoking §112, ¶6, the corresponding structure must be more than simply a general purpose computer or microprocessor; it must include the algorithm needed to transform the general purpose computer to a special purpose computer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An algorithm may be expressed as a mathematical formula, in prose, in a flowchart, or other manner providing sufficient structure. Mere reference to a general purpose computer with appropriate programming, or simply reciting 'software,' 'logic,' 'code,' or undefined computer components is insufficient. If no corresponding algorithm is disclosed, §112, ¶2 rejection is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of Algorithm Disclosure Judged in Light of Ordinary Skill
rubrics_metrics.description: If the specification discloses an algorithm, the sufficiency of that disclosure must be determined in light of the level of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner should determine whether one skilled in the art would know how to program the computer to perform the necessary steps (enablement) and whether the inventor was in possession of the invention (written description). The specification must sufficiently disclose the algorithm so a skilled person can implement it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mode of Implementation Limits Claim Scope (hardware vs software)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the supporting disclosure discusses hardware, software, or a combination, choosing a means-plus-function limitation limits the claim to the disclosed structure (hardware or hardware+software) and equivalents; examiner should not construe limitation as covering pure software implementation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no corresponding structure is disclosed (limitation supported only by software without algorithm), the limitation is indefinite and should be rejected under §112, ¶2. Consider claims as a whole when assessing whether a claim is directed to software per se.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner Must Establish a Clear Record When Issuing §112, ¶2 Rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should ensure the application file contains a complete and accurate picture of the Office’s consideration and provide clear explanations of actions taken during prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When rejecting under §112, ¶2, the examiner should clearly communicate findings and reasons supporting the rejection and avoid mere conclusory statements. MPEP §2173.05 provides examples of rationales (functional limitations, terms of degree, lack of antecedent basis, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Office Action Should Provide a Sufficient Explanation for Indefiniteness Rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office action must set forth the specific term or phrase that is indefinite and explain why the metes and bounds are unclear, providing enough information for the applicant to prepare a meaningful response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicate the specific term, explain in detail why it renders claim scope unclear, and whenever practicable, indicate how the indefiniteness issues may be resolved to overcome the rejection. Claims receive their broadest reasonable interpretation during prosecution to facilitate sharpening and clarifying.
